radicals.meaningMnemonic: A single drop (丶) is just water. But as soon as there are three, rising higher and higher, you know what's coming. A <radical>tsunami</radical>! Think of those drops as wave crests. Three whole tsunami waves, stacking up? That's a big tsunami.
See the slide going into the dirt? What appears to be a slide here is actually a <radical>coffin</radical>, sliding into the dirt to be buried.
You know <radical>Wolverine</radical> from the X-Men? He has three claws that come out of his hand whenever he needs to fight, not at all unlike the radical you see here.
You have 十 plus 十 (never mind that the left one is kinda curvy)... What do you get when you add these two kanji together? You get <radical>twenty</radical>.
This is the radical for <radical>meat</radical>. What's meat-like about this? Think of a nice square slab of meat with some beautiful 人-shaped marbling lines in it. Seeing it now? Mmm, meat.

Remember the eye radical? Imagine that's your eye now, and there's a drop of paint falling into it, making your eye color unique. Now it's what makes you you. It's what makes you your <radical>self</radical>.

In prison, dreaming in bed is the only way to see <radical>color</radical>. Picture a dark, dank cell with four gray walls. Now imagine the colorful dreamscapes your bed would take you to every night. What a contrast! That's why a prison bed = color.

You have the radicals for loiter, two, and barb. Someone who uses two barbs on you while you're loitering really wants you to <radical>GO</radical>!! GO on, stop loitering outside of my convenience store, ya dang kids!

You have the legs of a bird with wings outspread, landing in the mouth of her nest to rest. And when does she go back to rest? When the sun sets in the <radical>west</radical>! Imagine all the birds flying home as the sun sets. That's why this radical means west.

You could also see this as pi coming out of a mouth. Why would a mouth be talking about pi? Probably to figure out the curvature of the sun's path as it moves across the sky — to the west, always to the west!

This looks like something hooked around the corner of a mouth — it's a <radical>lip ring</radical>! Use your imagination, because it's either a giant lip ring or a very small mouth. It's angular because kanji prefer straight lines, but try to picture it as the kind of studded, angular lip ring your trendy friend wore in high school.
This radical is a <radical>scooter</radical>. See the handlebars and the little light? And there's a platform at the bottom you can stand or sit on (if it's one of those nice motorized scooters).

This is the radical for <radical>axe</radical>, since it looks like one. The two horizontal strokes are the head, the long left line is the whole edge of its blade, and the vertical line in the middle is its short handle. Kind of a strange axe, I admit, but an axe is an axe.
There are a bunch of lines coming out of a mouth. Think of them as speech lines in a little speech bubble. Those lines represent the things you <radical>say</radical>.

Underneath that hat are two bars of <radical>gold</radical>, but under those there are some spikes. This is some kind of trap for people who try to take your gold. And why else would you make a trap? Everyone wants to protect their gold.
The towel is getting soaked with drops of liquid. That's because it's <radical>rain</radical>ing. Get your towels and other clothes inside before they get soaked through from this rain!

If you find a rib cage on the moon, it'll probably be <radical>blue</radical>. Why? 'Cause it would have to come from one of the moon's inhabitants (the Moon People), and they're all blue — you know, due to the frigid temperatures and lack of oxygen and stuff.

See the <radical>mustache</radical> going around the mouth? Man, I wish I could grow a sweet mustache like this. (Sure, the mustache looks a lot like the head radical here, but just imagine it as a mustache this time!)
This is a very oddly shaped <radical>key</radical>, but it's a key nonetheless.

See the person running (to the right)? That's why this is the radical for <radical>run</radical>. Just don't confuse this with foot (足). The head in this one has streaks around it because the person is running so fast.

A rice paddy and some dirt — dirt roads, in fact, because this is a <radical>village</radical>. Small villages like this are mostly rice paddies and dirt (roads), you know? You could even think of this as a bird's-eye view of a village.

Under the hat there are two people <radical>meet</radical>ing in private. Look at them huddled up in there. They must have a reason to want to meet in such a private place, but that's not for you to judge. Maybe next time you have to meet with someone you'll hide under a hat with them too.

Think of an old-style <radical>lantern</radical>. It's in a box-shaped holder lined with rice paper and sits on four legs (you can only see two from this angle though). You can imagine people using these before electricity, right? That's why this radical is a lantern.
This radical already looks like a pair of rectangular <radical>feathers</radical>, right? I guess those short lines in each feather are like the filaments of the feathers.

Here we have the ground radical, with something underneath it. What likes lying in the ground, covered in mud? A <radical>pig</radical>! Use your imagination and see if you can find the head near the top, the piggy tail at the bottom right, and the little piglets on the left, nestling up to this mama pig.

When you're in prison, your only task is to count every <radical>angle</radical> in your cell. You count the angles of the walls and ceiling over and over again to pass the time. How many angles could there be in a room with four walls? Picture it and try to count those angles now.

See that lid on top? It's actually a flying saucer. "Take me to your leader," say the aliens inside, arriving from a strange-looking moon. When do you think you'd see something like this? At <radical>night</radical>. When people see UFOs or the moon, it's usually night. That's why this is the night radical.

On the top part of the head (冂) radical, there is a horn radical with one extra spike in the middle. This is a horned helmet with one extra spike. Who were famous for having horned helmets like that? The Vikings! That's why this radical is called <radical>Viking</radical>.

This looks like a stick-figure foot on the left kicking at something, which makes it the radical for <radical>kick</radical>. See the shin and foot swinging up for the kick? You can think of that part on the right as the edge of a ball that's about to be kicked.
This kinda looks like a spine with some rib bones, don't you think? That's why this is the radical for <radical>rib cage</radical>.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Who's someone who's just a <radical>mouth</radical> with <radical>legs</radical>? That's your know-it-all <kanji>older brother</kanji>, who won't shut up about anything.
kanji.meaningHint: To help this mnemonic along, literally imagine your older brother as someone that's just a giant mouth with a pair of legs walking around. It talks and talks and talks, too, irritating you. Feel the irritation specifically at your older brother. He's older than you, so you can't beat him up... yet.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You wish you could box your loud-mouth <kanji>older brother</kanji> up and send him far away to <reading>きょう</reading>と. きょうと is super far away from where you currently live, so just ship your older bro off so he can never bother you again.
kanji.readingHint: Hmm... don't you want to go to きょうと someday? Maybe you should have sent your brother somewhere less cool.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
The <radical>leader</radical> for the <radical>ceremony</radical> can't come so you need to find a <kanji>substitute</kanji> ASAP!

This kanji has another meaning too. The leader can't come to the ceremony because they fell through a time vortex into another <kanji>era</kanji>. They're trapped in a past era and don't know how to get back to the present, so a substitute will have to replace them in the ceremony.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture the substitute leader, looking all nervous as they get ready to lead the ceremony. Little do they know the real leader is fighting to survive in an ancient era.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>substitute</kanji> leader is wearing the wrong color clothes, so you have to <reading>dye</reading> (だい) them — just like they did in past <kanji>era</kanji>s.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine plunging your hands into a bucket full of dye and sloshing the substitute leader's clothing around in it, olden times-style. It's hard work, but it's not as bad as what the real leader's going through. Rather than dyeing, he's just dying… Dying to get back to the modern era!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You go down a <radical>slide</radical> made of <radical>branch</radical>es and your <kanji>skin</kanji> scrapes right off — ouch! Lucky for you, it was just your old outer layer of skin, and now you've got a fresh shiny layer. Yay for exfoliation! You're not sure what to do with this big, floppy layer of old skin, though…
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine sliding down a slide made of rough, gnarly tree branches. Their bark digs into your skin and pulls it right off of your body. Okay, it's painful, but it's a small price to pay for having such beautifully exfoliated skin.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Without your rough old <kanji>skin</kanji> to protect you, you feel the full <reading>he</reading>at (ひ) of the sun now. It burns… it burns! Yeah, you better protect that fresh new skin from the heat.
kanji.readingHint: Your skin usually protects you from the heat, but imagine how raw it would be after you shed the old layer all at once. It's kinda vulnerable right now, so take care of it.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You put a <radical>lid</radical> on your <radical>father</radical>. But, he won't taste good alone, so you <kanji>mix</kanji> in some other ingredients. They <kanji>mingle</kanji> inside the pot with him.
kanji.meaningHint: This may seem traumatic, but actually your father is surprisingly into it. Imagine him mixed in with all kinds of other things.
kanji.readingMnemonic: With a <kanji>mix</kanji> of your father and other ingredients <kanji>mingl</kanji>ing in your cooking pot, you lift up the lid... your father pops up. Your father is <reading>こう</reading>いち. He stares back at you with a big smile.
kanji.readingHint: "I love mixing in with potatoes and tomatoes," your father こういち states. "Turn up that temperature. I like to mingle with a bit more tingle."

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>meet</radical> radical and the <kanji>meet</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Know your radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: What better way to <kanji>meet</kanji> new people than to start <reading>kay</reading>aking (かい)! Get into your kayak and just float out into the water. You'll eventually bump into someone else in a kayak and boom, you're meeting someone new!
kanji.readingHint: "I met my soulmate in a kayak," said Koichi.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You see a <radical>triceratops</radical> in the distance. But, it's odd. It's perfectly <radical>pi</radical> shaped (that is, circular, like a pie). Some kind of piceratops, if you will. The reason they are this shape is because they want to absorb as much <kanji>light</kanji> as possible. They evolved to be round so they don't have any corners casting a shadow.
kanji.meaningHint: Absorbing light is natural for reptiles, and a round one can absorb even more. Imagine this strange, round piceratops basking in the warm rays of light shining down from the sky. What a rare sight you've come across.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you watch this majestic beast absorbing <kanji>light</kanji>, suddenly several dozen feral <reading>こう</reading>いちs burst out from the wilderness, spears in hand. Oh no! Those こういちs are hunting this rare piceratops!
kanji.readingHint: Imagine many different (but also kind of the same) こういちs attacking and throwing spears at the piceratops. Little do they know that it's fully charged up after absorbing all that light, and it unleashes a bright flash of energy, rendering all the こういちs momentarily blind and allowing it to escape.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>mustache</radical> on the <radical>ground</radical>. Upon closer inspection, you see that the mustache on the ground is exactly the <kanji>same</kanji> as yours!
kanji.meaningHint: Pick up the mustache, hold it up next to your face in front of a mirror. It's unbelievable, but it's the same in every way, down to the last hair.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
When we need to remember the reading どう, we use the word "doughnut".

While this is already strange enough, you notice something stranger. Over a couple feet away is a <reading>dou</reading>ghnut (どう) who also has the <kanji>same</kanji> mustache as you (and the one that fell on the ground). The doughnut looks at you for a moment, then scampers off. This doughnut must be a mutant because normally doughnuts don't move.
kanji.readingHint: If it helps, imagine hundreds or thousands of doughnuts all around you with the same exact mustache. First of all, it's terrifying to be surrounded by thousands of mutant doughnuts. Secondly, it's really weird they all have the same mustache as you.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There's a <radical>mouth</radical> inside a <radical>mouth</radical>. But if you look even closer (not actually, but we're pretending), you can see another mouth inside that mouth... and another one inside of that one! It keeps going and going. Can you count the number of <kanji>times</kanji> there's a mouth inside a mouth? This kanji also means <kanji>revolve</kanji> too. Think of each "time" a thing happens, it loops back around and comes back to the beginning, revolving around again another time.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine yourself counting and counting smaller and smaller mouths inside of each other, recording the number of times you can find a mouth inside another mouth. Dig deeper and deeper until it feels ridiculous how small the mouths are getting. Be sure to focus on the counting and the number of times you find one. Now, how many mouths is this times two, because your mouth is like this too.
kanji.readingMnemonic: If you're having a hard time wrapping your head around the infinite number of <kanji>times</kanji> these mouths <kanji>revolve</kanji>, just picture yourself in a little <reading>kay</reading>ak (かい) going around and down through the mouths.
kanji.readingHint: Your kayak is slashing and dipping through the revolving mouths, going down and down more times than you can count!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: How many <radical>evenings</radical> are there? There are <kanji>many</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: If you accidentally think "a lot" or something similar, that's okay too. It's the basic meaning that counts, and all these things are pretty close, though eventually you want to get to the point where you know that this kanji does in fact mean <kanji>many</kanji>.
kanji.readingMnemonic:
To remember the reading た we use the word "taco."

Let's start with the kanji meaning: <kanji>many</kanji>. You go outside in the evening (because that's what this kanji is made up of) and are surprised when you're hit by <kanji>many</kanji> <reading>ta</reading>cos (た) flying from the sky. For some reason it's raining tacos, and of course you have no idea why.
kanji.readingHint: The tacos pelt you and knock you off your feet. Hard shell, soft shell, meat, lettuce, tomatoes, cheese... it's terrible. And there are so many of them, flying from the sky to drown you in tacos. This is absolutely absurd (and you should think that too, so you remember the reading).

kanji.meaningMnemonic: What superhero is most like a <radical>triceratops</radical>? …If you said <radical>Wolverine</radical>, you're <kanji>correct</kanji>! Why is that the <kanji>right</kanji> answer? Because the triceratops has three horns, and Wolverine has three blades coming out of his hands. It's obvious, isn't it? But you knew that of course.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a triceratops. Now picture Wolverine. An equals sign between them. A little arrow pointing at the horns, an arrow pointing at the blades. And a big flashing CORRECT sign above them. Need I say more?
kanji.readingMnemonic: Because you got the answer <kanji>correct</kanji>, you win a free trip to <reading>とう</reading>きょう. Congrats!
kanji.readingHint: If you're lucky, you might see Wolverine fighting a triceratops in the middle of Shibuya Crossing in Tokyo. Heroes and monsters are always fighting in Tokyo, right? At least that's what my anime tells me.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>gun</radical> and you see some <radical>windows</radical>. What do you think you're going to do with this gun? Of course, you're going to shoot the windows... <kanji>every</kanji> single one of them. <kanji>Each</kanji> and every one.
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you get every one, and don't miss any of them. Actually search around in your imagination for any more windows, because you want to stress it's important you hit each and every window with your gun.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Now that <kanji>every</kanji> window is broken, you feel pretty stupid because <reading>mi</reading>ce (まい) are pouring in through <kanji>each</kanji> one. You've made a way for mice to get into your house. That wasn't smart.
kanji.readingHint: Now you need to shoot every one of the mice that came through those broken windows. You can't let any survive. You have to get every last one out of here!!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>rice</radical> radical and <kanji>rice</kanji> kanji are the same in looks and meaning. This kanji can also mean <kanji>America</kanji>, maybe because America is covered in rice or fields or something?
kanji.meaningHint: Aren't radicals nice? As nice and as fundamental as… rice. They make things so much easier, if you've been studying them.
kanji.readingMnemonic: A ton of <kanji>rice</kanji> is grown in <kanji>America</kanji>. And yet you never see rice in American cuisine. So where's all that unused rice going? Actually, it all gets dumped into a big <reading>bay</reading> (べい). They have too much rice and no place to store it, so they've started using bays to store it.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine helping to bulldoze the rice into the bay, watching it fill it up, then pile high. A bay isn't the best space for rice storage, but it'll do. The important thing is that you think you have way too much of the stuff, so the only way to get rid of it is to dump it in a large body of water, and that large body of water is a bay.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>feathers</radical> radical and <kanji>feather</kanji> kanji are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
kanji.meaningHint: Have you been studying your radicals? If so, this'll be easy!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You've gathered <kanji>feather</kanji> after feather, like some kind of wannabe birdman or birdwoman, and now you're ready to fly. But as soon as you're about to take off, someone dumps <reading>honey</reading> (はね) on you, making your feathers all goopy.
kanji.readingHint: Feel the honey in each feather, taste it trickling over your lips... And go ahead and plummet towards the ground (because you were jumping off a building to fly when someone doused you with honey). At least it's a tasty way to go, no?

kanji.meaningMnemonic: In a <radical>coffin</radical> there's a <radical>beggar</radical>, doing his begging. But it doesn't work, nobody helps him. So, he just begins to <kanji>think</kanji>: Why am I in this situation? How could I have avoided it? How will I get out? Think, dammit, think!!
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine him in his coffin, changing from a begging position to a stereotypical "thinking" position. His hand is on his chin, eyebrows furrowed. Focus on the beggar's thinking. This is a pretty abstract idea to imagine, so it will be important to create a vivid picture in your mind's eye.
kanji.readingMnemonic: What does the beggar <kanji>think</kanji> of? A thought bubble appears near his head. In it is a picture of <reading>こう</reading>いち! He's thinking that if こういち were here, he'd save him. Oh, if only こういち could save us all!
kanji.readingHint: Then, the beggar realizes that he is こういち. Here he is begging in a coffin, and still he only thinks of himself.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>meat</radical> radical and <kanji>meat</kanji> are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
kanji.meaningHint: Study those radicals, and perhaps we'll eat some meat tonight.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You know who loves <kanji>meat</kanji>? <reading>Nick</reading> (にく). You probably know a Nick — imagine him eating some succulent meat right now.
kanji.readingHint: If you don't know anyone named Nick, then just imagine it's Nic Cage. Picture him as he chews that succulent meat, maybe even closing his eyes in gastronomic ecstasy. Yeah. Go for it, Nic. Enjoy that meat.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>self</radical> radical and <kanji>self</kanji> are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
kanji.meaningHint: Radicals have self. Kanji have self. Kanji and radicals can sometimes be the same thing... so do they really have "self"? Only way to find out is to study both of them hard!
kanji.readingMnemonic:
When we need to remember じ we use the word "Jesus."

Who said you should always look at your <kanji>self</kanji> before tossing stones (or whatever) at others? <reading>Je</reading>sus (じ) did. So, make sure you look at your own self before being a jerk.
kanji.readingHint: You can feel free to do some introspection here.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>color</radical> radical and <kanji>color</kanji> are the same in looks as well as in meaning.
kanji.meaningHint: Color me pink! This kanji's super easy if you know your radicals.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You already have <kanji>color</kanji> on the mind because you know the meaning of this kanji, so think of something colorful about yourself. Imagine your <reading>ear</reading> (いろ) being a weird color... green, purple, red, whatever. Just make it really bright and standing out.
kanji.readingHint: You can even have someone ask you about your ear... "Is your ear okay? I think it's the color blue..."

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>go</radical> radical and the <kanji>go</kanji> kanji are exactly the same!
kanji.meaningHint: If you know your radicals well enough (and you do), you'll know this kanji.
kanji.readingMnemonic: "Oh, did he <vocabulary>go</vocabulary> again?" When <reading>こう</reading>いち is not around, that's what people often say because he goes to the <reading>gyo</reading>za (ぎょう) restaurant almost every day. こういち just loves gyoza so much, you always know where he is when he is not home.
kanji.readingHint: Remember, whenever we see the reading こう, think of こういち, a founder of WaniKani (who loves gyoza). We'll keep it consistent, so over time you should develop a character around こういち that you learn to love or hate.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>west</radical> radical and the <kanji>west</kanji> kanji are the same. Isn't that nice?
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you know all those radicals, it will make your life more pleasant.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You go off to the <vocabulary>west</vocabulary>. It's the Wild West, even. There aren't many people out here, making it easy to find a <reading>niche</reading> (にし) for your snake oil business.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the dusty, ramshackle towns in the Wild West where you find your niche. You set up shops with big signs that say SNAKE OIL. Congrats, you've cornered the snake oil niche in the Wild West!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Our <radical>leader</radical> has a <radical>lip ring</radical>. Wait, our leader has a lip ring? <kanji>WHAT</kanji>??
kanji.meaningHint: Think of our president (or your prime minister, or dictator, or whatever) and imagine this person appearing on television one morning with a big ol' lip ring. Feel surprised by it. Just say "What??" over and over again. You want to have the feeling of "what" in you when you imagine this — that'll help you to remember this kanji's meaning.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This leader with the lip ring wants one thing. <kanji>What</kanji> is it? A <reading>nanny</reading> (なに) who can make <reading>naan</reading> (なん). The leader loves naan because it's soft enough to eat with their lip ring on. And a nanny needs to make it because the leader can't do anything on their own.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine this leader calling the nanny over. "What is it?" asks the nanny. "Naan!" shouts the leader. What would that leader do without their naan nanny? What indeed.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical> has a <radical>book</radical> all about the human <kanji>body</kanji>. Knowing about bodies is a privilege. One that only leaders get—it helps them control all their subjects, like you.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine looking down at your body and thinking, huh, I wonder what all that junk is? Oh well, I'm sure the leader has it all figured out in that book of hers.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The leader's <kanji>body</kanji> book also taught her about something very body specific: how to tie a <reading>tie</reading> (たい). You can't have a tie on your body, no no. Those are for the leader and her smart body.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the leader, reading a book, putting a tie on her body. Look around at you and your family and your neighbors. You don't know what your body meat-bags do and you don't know how to tie a tie. Womp womp.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>leader</radical>'s <radical>key</radical> is the key that <kanji>make</kanji>s all the other keys. It's sort of like the one ring to rule them all, the one ring to bind them... except with keys.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine the leader taking his key to open up a safe that has a button to make other keys for the underlings. No key is as great as this key, though.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The leader <kanji>make</kanji>s all the keys and puts them in a <reading>sack</reading> (さく) to distribute them to the underlings, who then cut them into shape with a <reading>saw</reading> (さ).
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the leader making the keys and dropping them one by one into a big sack. He's always walking around carrying a big sack over his shoulder, distributing the keys to his underlings and watching them saw them into shape.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>mouth</radical> full of two massive <radical>drop</radical>s and… <radical>treasure</radical>?! Upon closer inspection, they appear to form some sort of <kanji>diagram</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Scientists have spent decades trying to figure out what the diagram of two massive drops and treasure in your mouth could mean, but to no avail. Imagine the pain of having to spend your entire life with a mouth full of two massive drops and treasure… poor you.
kanji.readingMnemonic: After decades of analyzing the <kanji>diagram</kanji>, scientists found out it leads to… a <reading>zoo</reading> (ず)?!
kanji.readingHint: Now you’re stuck at this zoo with your diagram mouth full of two massive drops and treasure. Scientists think this can't be it, so further research will be required. Your diagram mouth of drops and treasure isn't off the hook quite yet. Just a few more years, spent at this zoo! I promise!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>samurai</radical> with a <radical>flag</radical> on a <radical>stick</radical>. On his flag is the symbol 声, the kanji for <kanji>voice</kanji>. Why does he have that there? He feels like his shogun isn't giving him and his fellow samurai a voice, so he's brought a flag with the word "voice" written on it to protest.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine him and the other samurai with their flags on sticks, waving them around shouting things like "We want a voice!" and "Give us a voice!"
kanji.readingMnemonic: You decide to join the samurai's protest for more <vocabulary>voice</vocabulary> but immediately notice… they're all <reading>子, eh</reading> (こえ)?!
kanji.readingHint: Imagine your surprise at seeing this large protest of 子 samurai, shouting for their voices to be heard. Really make sure you can hear yourself going "You're a 子, eh?!" in your head.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: There is someone wearing <radical>horns</radical>, holding a <radical>bow</radical>, and going down a <radical>slide</radical> held up by a <radical>stick</radical>. What type of person do you imagine? I'd say someone who's an immature boy. That would be your <kanji>younger brother</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: If you don't have a younger brother, just pretend you do for now. Imagine him really vividly. He is a stereotypical little boy, playing dress-up with horns and a bow and arrow, and he's going down a makeshift slide held up by a stick.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>younger brother</kanji> loves playing dress-up so much that he's now started <reading>dye</reading>ing (だい) his hair all kinds of colors.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine the bright red, blue, green and purple dye in your younger brother's hair. He's put so much on that he's dyed half his face too. He's going to be in trouble when he gets home!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You're walking at night when you discover a <radical>lantern</radical> covered entirely in <radical>hair</radical>, making it a very strange <kanji>shape</kanji>. In fact, this is a <kanji>form</kanji> you'd never expect a lantern to take.
kanji.meaningHint: Picture all the different shapes this hairy lantern could take in your mind.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You stare at the <kanji>shape</kanji> until you finally recognize it: <reading>ca</reading>ke (けい)! Well, it's hairy, glowing cake, but it's still shaped like a big slice of cake.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the shape of this hairy, glowing cake.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>ground</radical> is scattered with <radical>rice</radical>, which will cause the Predator to <kanji>come</kanji> because he loves rice. Then once he's gone, the <kanji>next</kanji> Predator will come to eat.
kanji.meaningHint: This kanji kind of looks like a Predator face, so just imagine Predators come whenever the ground is scattered with rice. They come from all around to grab handfuls of it. Who's next, then? Come forward!
kanji.readingMnemonic: When they come, though, they're all disappointed. It turns out it's <reading>rye</reading> (らい) grains, and rye grains taste terrible. Yuck.
kanji.readingHint: If you love rye grains, on the other hand, imagine them being really happy that they came to get the rice. They're so lucky it's rye!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Plant a <radical>spirit</radical> in the <radical>dirt</radical> before you start your <kanji>company</kanji> and it will be successful. That's what all the great, old Japanese companies did back in the olden days. That's why companies like Mitsubishi have been around for hundreds of years. They planted a spirit in the dirt to help their company grow, and grow it did!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a young person way back in old-timey history times burying the spirit of one of their ancestors in the dirt. Now watch as an old-timey time lapse plays out in front of your eyes and a company is born!
kanji.readingMnemonic: Where did you learn about this method of <kanji>company</kanji> growing? From a <reading>sha</reading>man (しゃ), of course. Shamans aren't just spouting nonsense, they know what they're talking about. And spirits are right up their shaman alley.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine going to a shaman and having them tell you that for your company to be successful you need to bury a spirit in the dirt so it can help the company grow. You should probably listen.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>angle</radical> radical and the <kanji>angle</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: You gotta know your radicals first! Only then can you start to study these kanji from other angles — meanings, readings, all that good stuff. One angle at a time, you know?
kanji.readingMnemonic: To see those kanji angles from every <kanji>angle</kanji>, you <reading>cock</reading> (かく) your head to the side.
kanji.readingHint: Kinda like how a dog cocks its head at an angle when it's trying to understand what you say. That's what you look like when you're studying radicals! Aww, you're so cute.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>say</radical> radical and the <kanji>say</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Know your radicals, yo!
kanji.readingMnemonic: If you aren't sure what to <kanji>say</kanji>, just think about <reading>Gen</reading>ji (げん) and ask yourself, "What would Genji say?"
kanji.readingHint: Genji is a real smooth talker. In fact, he can talk his way out of anything. If you can just stay calm and think "What would Genji say?" before saying anything, you'll probably end up saying something cool instead of something lame.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: <radical>Fins</radical> decorate a <radical>hat</radical>, with (presumably fish) <radical>mouths</radical> stitched to it. Who wears strange hats like this? Turns out, the <kanji>valley</kanji> people are the ones who wear these. I'm talking about the "Valley Girls" of Los Angeles, California. They're into the crazy fashion, and they'll wear anything if it's deemed "cool" or something like that.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a bunch of Valley Girls walking around with these strange hats. Fins and fish mouths... what a strange new fad.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Hanging around with all the <kanji>Valley</kanji> Girls in the sunny area of LA is also a robot. It's WALL-E's distant (and lazy, lounging) relative, <reading>TAN-E</reading> (たに). He sits around getting a tan in LA with the Valley Girls while his cousin picks up trash.
kanji.readingHint: What a jerk he is. Imagine the deep tan lines on TAN-E as well. He's the epitome of robot laziness.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical <radical>run</radical> and the kanji <kanji>run</kanji> are exactly the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you know your radicals!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You <kanji>run</kanji> and run and run and suddenly you feel your <reading>sou</reading>l (そう) leave your body. Still running, you turn around and see your soul running a few steps behind you.
kanji.readingHint: Running really takes it out of you. In this case, it takes your soul out of you. Don't worry, when you stop your soul will collide with you again and everything will be okay. (Probably.)

kanji.meaningMnemonic: Someone on a <radical>scooter</radical> has an <radical>axe</radical>, and they're getting <kanji>near</kanji> to you really fast! Oh no, they're so <kanji>close</kanji> now, you need to get out of here!
kanji.meaningHint: Picture a scooter coming toward you in the dark. You see the gleam of the axe as it looms nearer and nearer.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As they draw <kanji>near</kanji>, you recognize who is riding the scooter: the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England! Behind him, a bunch of his guards also on scooters and wielding axes appear and move <kanji>close</kanji> to you.
kanji.readingHint: The King is now so near to you his nose and mustache are tickling your face. He's holding the axe high above his head and saying, "I can get as close to you as I want and you can't stop me because I'm the King. I can get sooooo close. Look, I'm not touching you though!"

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>village</radical> you always think of first is your <kanji>hometown</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Why would you ever talk about the village where someone else was born? Answer: you wouldn't. Everything is always about you.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Your <kanji>hometown</kanji> is where you <reading>sat</reading> (さと), nostalgia tugging at your heartstrings amid the endless rice fields and dirt.
kanji.readingHint: Visualize yourself sitting in your hometown, the village's rustic charm evoking nostalgia.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You know what really sticks to your <radical>rib cage</radical> in the <radical>winter</radical>? <kanji>Wheat</kanji>! There's nothing like a hearty diet of wheat bread, Wheaties, and cream of wheat to get you through the tough winter months.
kanji.meaningHint: Smell the sweet, nutty aroma of wheat filling your home as you stockpile bags of the stuff to turn into bread and cereal. This winter might not be so bad, after all.
kanji.readingMnemonic: As you fill your home with <kanji>wheat</kanji>, it starts to get <reading>muggy</reading> (むぎ). You're in a small, enclosed area baking lots of bread and boiling a bunch of water for cream of wheat, so it's only natural that it would start to get pretty muggy in there.
kanji.readingHint: You don't mind the mugginess, though — your muggy, wheat-filled house is actually pretty cozy during these cold, dry winter months.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a wild <radical>viking</radical> <radical>child</radical> you have to take care of. He won't do anything but <kanji>study</kanji>, surprisingly. You can't get him to eat, use the bathroom, or anything else. He just wants to study.
kanji.meaningHint: Of course, this isn't what you'd expect of a little viking child. It's the opposite. That's why it's so surprising! He loves to study!
kanji.readingMnemonic: This crazy viking child who prefers <kanji>study</kanji> over pillaging (and other viking activities)... the other vikings just stop and <reading>gawk</reading> (がく) at him when they walk by.
kanji.readingHint: You should tell the other vikings to stop gawking at this child. Just because he likes to study doesn't mean he's a bad viking...

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You have a <radical>tree</radical> and another <radical>tree</radical>. You basically have yourself a <kanji>forest</kanji>!
kanji.meaningHint: Follow the logic of this one and you should be okay.
kanji.readingMnemonic: So, now you have this <kanji>forest</kanji> and you want to cut it down (so much money!). But, you don't have any tools, only your hands. You think... I've done karate for a while, so I can probably chop it down that way. You get in a chopping stance, then do your battle cry and hit: "<reading>HAYA... SHI******</reading> (はやし)!"
kanji.readingHint: Obviously that didn't work well — you'll want to focus on your battle cry plus indecent swearing right afterwards to remember this reading.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: What was the biggest <radical>hole</radical> in the <radical>construction</radical> of the world? The <kanji>sky</kanji>. If you think about it, the sky is like a big hole someone forgot to fill in. That's why this kanji also means <kanji>empty</kanji>! Makes sense — nothing is more empty than the sky.
kanji.meaningHint: Next time you look up at the sky, try to imagine it's a big empty hole you're stuck at the bottom of.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>sky</kanji> is usually empty until clouds stage a <reading>coup</reading> (くう). Basically you can think of the sky as the site for one coup after another as the weather changes.
kanji.readingHint: First the sky's cloudy, then it's clear and empty, then overcast again... Just coup after coup!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>gold</radical> radical and the <kanji>gold</kanji> kanji are the same!
kanji.meaningHint: Just know your radicals and you'll be golden, so to speak.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The most <kanji>gold</kanji> in the land belongs to the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England. In fact, you've never actually met someone with gold, it all goes straight to the King whenever someone finds some. You just have a few pennies to work with.
kanji.readingHint: Picture the King on a huge pile of gold. Gold coins, gold candelabras, gold ponies. He's laughing and pointing at all of it while making very strong eye contact with you.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The radical for <radical>rain</radical> and the kanji for <kanji>rain</kanji> are the same thing.
kanji.meaningHint: Make sure you know your radicals!
kanji.readingMnemonic: What if the <kanji>rain</kanji> actually tried to <reading>aim</reading> (あめ) for you? As in, drops would move out of their normal flight path just to hit you on your head? You'd be a lot wetter, that's for sure.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine a world where each rain drop had to choose a target to aim for. How strange would rainfall be? Also, あめ and "aim" don't really sound too much alike, but the goal is to use "aim" to get to あめ, so make sure to take note of that in your mind as you learn the reading.

kanji.meaningMnemonic:
The <radical>blue</radical> radical and the <kanji>blue</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.

Additionally, this can also mean <kanji>young</kanji>. You can remember this because young people have potential as limitless as the blue sky!
kanji.meaningHint: Don't feel blue, you should know this kanji automagically!
kanji.readingMnemonic: You've been feeling really <kanji>blue</kanji>. Mostly because your skin, hair, and eyes have all turned blue. It was an out-of-the-blue transformation! But now someone places his hand on your shoulder and points at your <reading>sa</reading>ber (せい). It's blue too! You aren't alone!
kanji.readingHint: You aren't sure how you or the saber turned blue, but at least you and your saber are a good match now, I guess.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: You plant your <radical>flowers</radical> in the light of the <radical>sun</radical> in the shape of a <radical>cross</radical>, but it's too hot — the sun is too strong — and you end up with <kanji>grass</kanji>. Flowers can't grow in these conditions.
kanji.meaningHint: Think of how disappointed you are. You wanted a beautiful cross of flowers, and now you just have a big overgrown patch of thick grass. It isn't even pretty green grass, it's a little brown and damaged from the sun.
kanji.readingMnemonic: The <kanji>grass</kanji> on top is brown and burned from the sun, so you need to take a <reading>cool saw</reading> (くさ) and hack the tops off. The saw is actually physically cool to the touch, to help heal the grass's sunburned bits. It just happens to look cool too.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine using your cool saw to saw off the heads of all of this grass. You made the cross pretty big, so there is a ton of grass to get through. The sun is beating down on you and the grass too, which isn't making it any easier.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: For some reason, you are <radical>stand</radical>ing on the <radical>sun</radical>. It's obviously very hot, but the thing you notice most is the <kanji>sound</kanji> of you burning up.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine a super loud sizzling sound, drowning everything else out. It's ridiculously loud, and hurts your ears more than the sun's heat hurts your skin.
kanji.readingMnemonic: This <kanji>sound</kanji> isn't just loud, it's familiar. Finally you place it: <reading>on</reading>ions (おん)!
kanji.readingHint: Your burning body sounds just like sizzling, crispy onions being fried in a pan. Listen close. It's exactly the same! You can almost smell onions too!

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>night</radical> radical and the <kanji>night</kanji> kanji are exactly the same.
kanji.meaningHint: All those late nights studying radicals really pay off, you know.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You call your friend at <kanji>night</kanji> and say "<reading>Yo, Lou</reading> (よる)!"
kanji.readingHint: Lou is a total night owl, so you only hit him up at night.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: When the <radical>moon</radical> is bright, it's easy to see that a <radical>pig</radical> is indeed a <kanji>pig</kanji>.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine walking outside at night and seeing a strange oinking animal. You think it's a pig, but just to be sure you grab that thing and hold it up to the moonlight. Yes, definitely a pig! Now you know.
kanji.readingMnemonic: Legend has it that if you catch a <kanji>pig</kanji> in moonlight, it will tell you its secrets. Sure enough, this pig tells you it's from <reading>Bhuta</reading>n (ぶた).
kanji.readingHint: A pig from Bhutan?! Yes, all pigs are actually from Bhutan, it whispers. Then this Bhutan pig escapes your grip and trots off into the moonlight.

kanji.meaningMnemonic: The <radical>axe</radical> radical and the <kanji>axe</kanji> kanji are exactly the same, with one minor difference. This kanji is also used as the <kanji>bread loaf counter</kanji>, probably because bread was so big and hard in the past that they had to use axes to slice them.
kanji.meaningHint: Imagine you've gone back in time a good hundred years, and you're trying to count loaves of bread after each swing of your axe. Axes and bread loaves will become intertwined in your brain.
kanji.readingMnemonic: You imagined being back in time too good and now you're stuck using an <kanji>axe</kanji> to be a <kanji>bread loaf counter</kanji> for the <reading>Kin</reading>g (きん) of England. You aren't sure which king he is or when in time you are, but he's mean and keeps eating all the bread you cut up with your axe.
kanji.readingHint: Imagine being stuck using an axe on bread while the King of England glares down at you, munching and spilling crumbs everywhere.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji 入 means "enter," but this word does not mean "to enter" (which you already learned as 入る). Still, the meaning of 入れる is still related to the kanji's meaning: it means <vocabulary>to insert</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to put in</vocabulary>. It's something you do to another object, like inserting a key into a lock, or your hand into a glove.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
When a vocab is a single kanji plus some okurigana (hiragana stuck on the end of kanji) it's almost always going to be the kun'yomi reading. This is one of two kun'yomi readings you'll be learning for the kanji 入. As long as you know that this vocab means <vocabulary>to insert</vocabulary>, you can use that to remember the reading as well. 

Imagine inserting your hand into a hole and an <reading>ea</reading>gle (い) flies out, screaming: "<reading>い</reading>!" This is something that happens every time you insert your hand into something: an eagle comes out. You don't know why.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>above</kanji>, and this verb means <vocabulary>to go up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rise</vocabulary>.

It's an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. For example: Prices go up. Temperatures rise. See? No direct object. You can remember this because stock prices always seems to go up when you see this one <reading>girl</reading> (がる). You don't know how this girl makes stock prices go up, she just does. Think of her as your lucky girl.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you can guess that it uses the kun'yomi reading. You've learned that reading, but here's a mnemonic in case you need a refresher:

You know this word means <vocabulary>to go up</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to rise</vocabulary>. Imagine just rising into the air, sort of floating up all of a sudden. What would you say? You'd probably scream "<ja><reading>Ah</reading></ja> (あ)!" the moment you started to go up. You know, out of surprise. Going up? Ah!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>below</kanji>, and 下がる means <vocabulary>to get lower</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>to go down</vocabulary>.

It's an intransitive verb, so it doesn't take a direct object. For example: Prices fall. Temperatures come down. See? No direct object. You can remember this because your fever always goes down when a certain <reading>girl</reading> (がる) takes care of you. Imagine a kind, caring girl making you chicken soup and giving you medicine and stuff — your fever would have no choice but <vocabulary>to come down</vocabulary>. (Also, this girl is probably your mom.)
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word has okurigana (hiragana attached to the kanji) you know that it's probably going to use the kun'yomi reading. Let's use a mnemonic to remember the reading of the kanji:

You were running a fever, but now your temperature has started <vocabulary>to get lower</vocabulary>. Why? Because you used a <reading>saw</reading> (さ). With your trusty saw, you did some good old-fashioned bloodletting, medieval doctor-style, and now your fever is really starting to come down. Actually, your blood pressure and oxygen levels have come down too… um, WAY down. Maybe using this saw wasn't such a good idea after all…

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. You already learned that 出る means "to exit," and this is the transitive version of that. In other words, you're doing the action of causing something else to exit, so this word means to take out. When you take something out, you're making it exit where it previously was, right? 出す is a super versatile word that can also mean to turn in (an assignment, for example), to put out something (like the garbage or recycling), or to let out something (a sigh, a sound, or even a bodily fluid). It can also be a casual term for paying for something, since you're taking out your cash and handing it over.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
The だ reading is the part you want to remember here, so here's a mnemonic to help you out:

Your favorite thing <vocabulary>to take out</vocabulary> is your <reading>da</reading>d's (だ) credit card. You take it out whenever it's time for a shopping spree — which is all the time, basically. Your dad's okay with this, although you sometimes cause him <vocabulary>to let out</vocabulary> a wail when he sees his monthly statement. Thanks, Daddy — love you!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "life" so what is the verb form of that? Would it be "to do life"? No, probably not. In this case it is <vocabulary>to give birth</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to produce</vocabulary>.

You'll have to differentiate this one from the word 生まれる as well. Just remember that when you give birth, you're the one who has to actually <reading>mo</reading>ve (む) your body by finding the right position and pushing with every ounce of strength you can muster. In contrast, when you're being born, you can just kind of lie there and enjoy the ride.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
You have to remember the う part of this word to be able to read it. You already learned this reading with 生まれる, but here's a mnemonic for you just in case you forgot: 

Imagine yourself giving birth, but not to a baby. Instead, it's an <reading>u</reading>ni (う) you're delivering. Luckily, uni aren't fully formed with their spikes at birth so it shouldn't be a problem. Ooof! What a relief!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means "stand" and this means <vocabulary>to stand something up</vocabulary>. It also can mean <vocabulary>to make something</vocabulary>, both in a physical sense, like making a sound, and a mental sense, like making a plan. 

Don't confuse this with 立つ. 立てる means that you're standing something up. As in, "I stood up the action figure" or "I will erect the flag." You're doing the action to something else.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You already learned the kun'yomi reading for this kanji with 立つ, so you should be good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word means <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary>, which might surprise you if you remember that the kanji 分 means <kanji>part</kanji>. Think of it this way: to understand something you have to break it down into its parts to see how it works.

Watch out, though, because whereas in English you understand something, in Japanese the thing you understand is the grammatical subject (it's doing the action). So, a more literal meaning for this is <vocabulary>to be understandable</vocabulary>. In other words, there's no object, and 分かる is intransitive, meaning it happens on its own. The かる ending is a hint, because verbs with かる as okurigana (kana added to the kanji) are usually intransitive.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You didn't learn that reading with this kanji, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Whenever you try <vocabulary>to understand</vocabulary> something, you just start screaming "<reading>WAAAAAAAAAHHHH</reading>" (わ). It helps you focus and concentrate on what you’re trying to understand, to the dismay of everyone around you. WAAAAAAAAAHHHH.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji means <kanji>stop</kanji>, so the verb 止まる means <vocabulary>to stop</vocabulary>. 

But this is the intransitive version, so it doesn't take a direct object. A train stops, or you stop at a red light. See? No direct object. You can remember this because you often have to stop when you see a 丸 (まる), a.k.a. a circle. Think about it — red lights, the cancel symbol, and no trespassing signs are all 丸. Even stop signs are… sort of 丸?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading when you learned the 止める, so you should be able to read it already!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well. This implies that it is your older brother, by the way. Not somebody else's.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Your <vocabulary>older brother</vocabulary> is different from everyone else's. He has odd powers... some would say powers of the force. Do you know what his name is? It's <reading>Ani</reading> (あに), short for Anikin... wait a sec, does that sound familiar?

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: What do you think a <kanji>fat</kanji> <kanji>letter</kanji> is? If I were to guess, I'd say a <vocabulary>bold letter</vocabulary>. You know, like <vocabulary>bold text</vocabulary> on a screen.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this one is a bit odd. It combines the kun'yomi ふと from 太 with the on'yomi じ from 字. You learned both these readings with the kanji, so you should be OK here. You'll just have to remember it's a weird mix of kun'yomi and on'yomi. It kind of makes this word stand out… as if it were written in bold letters.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>see</kanji>, and 見える is <vocabulary>to be visible</vocabulary>, or <vocabulary>to be in sight</vocabulary>, though it's often more naturally translated into English as <vocabulary>can see</vocabulary>. It's used when you don't actively intend to see something, it just happens.

This verb can also mean <vocabulary>to seem</vocabulary>, when talking about how you perceive something you can see.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned with the kanji (the kun'yomi reading). So as long as you know that you should be able to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.

皮 refers to <vocabulary>skin</vocabulary> as something separate from the body. You can use 皮 for when your skin starts to peel off with sunburn, or for animal skin when it is being stripped off or turned into a <vocabulary>hide</vocabulary>. You can also use 皮 to describe the outer layer of fruits and vegetables, like apple skins or banana <vocabulary>peel</vocabulary>s.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
Since this word is made up of a single kanji, it should use the kun'yomi reading. You haven't learned this reading yet, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

As a human (we think), you have a lot of <vocabulary>skin</vocabulary>. But sometimes a normal shower isn't enough to wash all that skin. What do you do when you can't fit all your skin in the shower or the tub? You get your skin cleaned at the <reading>ca</reading>r <reading>wa</reading>sh, of course!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This word consists of kanji with hiragana attached. Because the hiragana ends with an う sound, you know this word is a verb. The kanji itself means <kanji>mix</kanji> so the verb version is <vocabulary>to mix something</vocabulary>. 

It’s transitive, so you’re doing the mixing. With this word, the things you’ve mixed are still distinguishable from each other. Two types of fish in your aquarium, books of different genres on your shelf — that kind of thing.

There's a の particle stuck in the middle of this word. Here it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after. 

But for now, all you really have to remember is that 男の子 means "boy."
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: If you know the kun'yomi readings of both of these kanji you should be okay. You have two separate single-kanji words put together by a の. That's why it's the kun'yomi reading - they're separate.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you think of a <kanji>fur</kanji> <kanji>insect</kanji> what do you think of? My mind immediately goes to a <vocabulary>caterpillar</vocabulary>. Imagine the furriest caterpillar you can and touch it. How does it feel? Furry?
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings for this word are strange. Both use the kun'yomi readings - 虫 uses the reading you learned with the kanji, so that's easy. The 毛 part is like the vocab word 毛 you learned in the previous lesson.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have the <kanji>below</kanji> <kanji>town</kanji>. Does this sort of sound familiar? We have another word for it in English, but it's essentially the same thing: <vocabulary>downtown</vocabulary>. It isn't the downtown you might be used to though. In Japan, this is an old word that was used for the commercial districts literally, physically down (lower than) the main city. So picture an old, urban Japanese area!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is all kun'yomi despite being jukugo. Just think of sketchy things going on in the downtown, just like how there's sketchy kun'yomi readings for this word. You should know both the kun'yomi readings from the previous level, though, so if you do you know the reading for this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
A <kanji>man</kanji> <kanji>person</kanji> is a <vocabulary>man</vocabulary>. 

There's a の particle stuck in the middle of this word. Here it just means the noun before の is modifying the noun after. 

Don't worry if that's hard to remember though. Just remember 男の人 means "man" (and that it's more polite than plain 男).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 4 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You know that 今 means now. What you probably don't know is that まで means "until." So, this word means <vocabulary>until now</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the kun'yomi reading which you learned previously when you learned the vocab word 今. You can tell this is a kun'yomi reading because it has hiragana attached. So if you know that, you should be able to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: When you have <kanji>fur</kanji> <kanji>string</kanji> (aka string made of fur) what do you think of? Hopefully <vocabulary>wool yarn</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings for these kanji are the kun'yomi readings. With 毛 you should have learned this reading via the vocab word in the previous level. With 糸 it's actually the main reading for the kanji, so you should already know it.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You'll have to learn this word in two parts. You already know the meaning of 今 because of the kanji, which means "now." The すぐ part, however, is a new word, meaning "soon." すぐ and "soon" even start with a similar sound, so maybe that can help you remember this! If you put 今 and すぐ together, you get "now soon." Put in better English, that's <vocabulary>at once</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>right now</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since you already know the vocab word 今 (read いま), you should be able to read this word as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
This is the village you came from. This is where your parents live. This is your <vocabulary>hometown</vocabulary> (same meaning as the kanji you learned).

This word is old-fashioned and evokes a warm, nostalgic image of home. Often seen in folktales and traditional songs, it represents an idyllic, pastoral life.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as with the kanji you learned, so you should feel nice and "at home" with this one 😉

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You have your <kanji>home village</kanji> and your <kanji>heart</kanji>. Your heart always resides in your home village, so when you leave you feel <vocabulary>homesick</vocabulary>.

Young people don't really use this word anymore. It's more for the oldies. If you're an oldie, go right ahead. If you're a youngie, then talk to more oldies!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The readings are double kun'yomi. The kun'yomi reading is what you learned with 里 already, though you'll have to pull out the 心 vocab reading to remember it all. Not only that, the 心 gets rendaku'd here making it ごころ. Make sure you watch out for that.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: What is <kanji>real</kanji> is <kanji>right</kanji>. It is the <vocabulary>reality</vocabulary>. It is also the <vocabulary>truth</vocabulary>. Don't believe anything that isn't <vocabulary>real</vocabulary> and <vocabulary>true</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Reading is the same as what you learned with the kanji.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
You learned 空 means "sky," but it can also mean "empty." An <kanji>empty</kanji> <kanji>car</kanji> literally means "empty car," but in practice, you'll usually see this lit up on a taxi to mean <vocabulary>open taxi</vocabulary>. If you spot it, feel free to hail it down!

You might also see 空車 at a parking lot. In that case, it means there's an <vocabulary>empty parking space</vocabulary> available.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you often <kanji>think</kanji> about <kanji>study</kanji>ing <kanji>old</kanji> things, it's called <vocabulary>archeology</vocabulary>. All archeology involves thinking about old things, at least a little bit.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
<kanji>One</kanji> <kanji>life</kanji> is all you get. It's your <vocabulary>whole life</vocabulary>. This can also mean <vocabulary>all one's life</vocabulary>, and when it's used as an adjective it means <vocabulary>lifelong</vocabulary>.

一生 is about life as a span of time: your whole life from start to finish. You'll see it in phrases like 一生の友人 (a lifelong friend) or 一生わすれない (to never forget something for the rest of one's life).
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word that uses on'yomi readings of the kanji. You didn't learn this reading for 生 though, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

Who has been in charge of you your <vocabulary>whole life</vocabulary>? The <reading>sho</reading>gun (しょう).

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Things you end up <kanji>doing</kanji> in the <kanji>grass</kanji> and not inside probably take a lot of big <vocabulary>gesture</vocabulary>s and <vocabulary>action</vocabulary>s. You have to do them outside on the grass because if you did them anywhere else you might break something.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: The reading is a combination of on'yomi and kun'yomi. That being said, both readings for both kanji are the readings you learned with the kanji so you should be able to read this. Just watch out because rendaku makes くさ become ぐさ.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word share one of the same meanings: <vocabulary>form</vocabulary>. It doesn't just mean form though, it means <vocabulary>tense</vocabulary> too. Like verb tense.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You want to <kanji>mix</kanji> opinions from <kanji>outside</kanji> your country into the way you handle things. That's called <vocabulary>diplomacy</vocabulary>. If you mix your country with the ones outside of your own, you'll all profit!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how you learned that 生まれる means "to be born?" Well once you're born that place where it happened becomes your <vocabulary>birthplace</vocabulary>!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: Since this word consists of a kanji with hiragana attached, you can bet that it will use the kun'yomi reading. You learned this reading when you learned 生まれる. Just drop the る off the end and you have your reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If all you can see is the <kanji>big</kanji> <kanji>body</kanji> of something, then you'll only get a <vocabulary>general</vocabulary> idea of what it is. You'll be able to say that it's <vocabulary>generally</vocabulary> a certain way, but that's <vocabulary>about</vocabulary> all. You'll get the <vocabulary>gist</vocabulary>, but no more.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 大 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

<vocabulary>Generally</vocabulary>, it's a bad idea to <reading>dye</reading> your <reading>tie</reading>s (だいたい). The tie police isn't a big fan of it, and you wouldn't wanna get arrested!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: If you <kanji>study</kanji> <kanji>writing</kanji>, it's called <vocabulary>literature</vocabulary>. You'll get to study lots of things other people wrote before you!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. Since 文 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use:

All the great works of <vocabulary>literature</vocabulary> are about <reading>bun</reading>s (ぶん). That's the subtle thread running through all literature: buns.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You want to talk about the <kanji>origin</kanji> where something <kanji>come</kanji>s from. That's where it is from <vocabulary>originally</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word that uses the on'yomi readings of the kanji. You should be able to read this on your own.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: This has the 〜 for counters, so you can bet this shares the <vocabulary>bread loaf counter</vocabulary> meaning with the kanji.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has the same reading as the kanji you learned, meaning you know the reading!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: その means "that" or "the", and その plus <kanji>other</kanji> means things like <vocabulary>the others</vocabulary>, <vocabulary>other</vocabulary>, and <vocabulary>other than that</vocabulary>, depending on the context.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This has two readings, but luckily you learned one of them when you learned the kanji, and the other one when you learned the word 他. The two readings are usually interchangeable, too.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember 北口 from a couple levels ago, and how 入り口 means "entrance" and 出口 means "exit?" Combine that 口 meaning with the kanji for <kanji>west</kanji>, and you get <vocabulary>west exit</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>west entrance</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This follows the same pattern as 入り口, 出口, and 北口, so it uses kun'yomi readings. And just like with those, make sure to watch out for the rendaku that changes くち to ぐち!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: What's a "third day moon"? It's a <vocabulary>crescent moon</vocabulary>. A crescent moon is the newly visible moon that appears on the third day of the month in the lunar calendar that Japanese people used back in the day.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word combines the vocab words 三日 and 月, so it uses their readings, except they're slightly different here: there's no small っ in 三日, and 月 has rendaku. Sounds complicated, but the changes actually make the word easier to pronounce. (Try it yourself — みかづき is easier to say than みっかつき, right?) Here's a mnemonic to remember the みか and づ parts, just in case:

You're out with your friend Mika one night when a <vocabulary>crescent moon</vocabulary> appears. What do you say to her? "<reading>Mika</reading>, <reading>du</reading>de (みかづ)! It's a crescent moon!" 

Hint: To get the character づ, type "du" on your keyboard.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Remember how 上手 means that you're <vocabulary>good at</vocabulary> something? Well, this word uses the exact same kanji, and means the exact same thing!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
That い on the end is your clue that the reading is different, and you can forget about the readings you learned for each kanji. This is a native Japanese word, and the kanji were assigned to it based on the meaning alone. That means you just have to memorize the reading, so here's a mnemonic to help you:

When you see that someone's <vocabulary>good at</vocabulary> something, you say, "<reading>Ooh</reading>, <reading>my</reading> (うまい)!" at the top of your lungs. Try it! Think of something that impresses you and say "ooh my!" out loud.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: You have the number "thirty", and <kanji>age</kanji>. So this refers to <vocabulary>one's thirties</vocabulary>.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This uses on'yomi for all the kanji, so you should be good to go here!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
When you buy something, you basically <kanji>substitute</kanji> it with <kanji>money</kanji>. That substitute money is the <vocabulary>cost</vocabulary> or <vocabulary>price</vocabulary> of the thing you're paying for.

There are a lot of money-related synonyms in Japanese, but keep in mind this one refers to the money you pay to get some stuff in return (usually goods), not to an expense, price, or value. It's "substitute money" after all!
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which means it uses on'yomi readings for both of the kanji. You already know those, so you should be good to go!

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic: Find a <kanji>flat</kanji> surface and <kanji>go</kanji> along it. Now you are running <vocabulary>parallel</vocabulary> to it.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

vocabulary.meaningMnemonic:
When do things begin to go in the <kanji>evening</kanji> <kanji>direction</kanji>? That would be in the <vocabulary>early evening</vocabulary> or simply the <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary>.

夕方 refers to the period of the day between afternoon and nighttime, when the sun is starting to go down and it's gradually beginning to get darker outside.
vocabulary.readingMnemonic:
This word uses the kun'yomi readings for both kanji. You learned 夕's kun'yomi reading with the kanji, so you should be okay there. The 方 reading wasn't the main one learned, though, and plus it's rendaku'd, so here's a mnemonic to help you remember it:

<vocabulary>Early evening</vocabulary> is your curfew — you <reading>gotta</reading> (がた) be home by then. If you're out past <vocabulary>evening</vocabulary>, you'll miss dinner and get in trouble, so you gotta head home as soon as it starts getting dark. You GOTTA!
